name: Facial nerve rehab / neurectomy
lead: Facial nerve rehabilitation and neurectomy refer to medical and surgical approaches for facial asymmetry caused by facial nerve paralysis. Rehabilitation involves therapy and exercise techniques, and surgical options include nerve repair, grafting, nerve transfers and muscle transfers. Neurectomy means cutting or removing part of a nerve.

Facial paralysis has many causes. Bell's palsy is the most common cause of acute onset, and others include infections such as Lyme disease and Ramsay Hunt syndrome, trauma, tumours, stroke and congenital conditions.[1] About 71% of Bell's palsy patients are reported to recover fully.[1]

In looksmaxxing discussion the topic appears as a treatment for paralysis-induced asymmetry rather than as an enhancement for people with typical faces. The sources reviewed contain no looksmaxxing-community material on it.

paras: Bell's palsy, of unknown cause but associated with herpes simplex infection, is the most common cause of acute facial paralysis. Other causes include Lyme disease, reactivation of varicella zoster virus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome), middle ear infection, temporal bone fractures, acoustic neuromas and parotid tumours, diabetes, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and Moebius syndrome, which is present at birth. Stroke produces a central facial palsy that spares the forehead.[1]

For Bell's palsy, corticosteroids are used, with antivirals added in severe cases, and eye protection with artificial tears, ointment and taping during sleep. Corticosteroids begun within three days of onset are reported to improve the chance and speed of recovery.[1]

Surgical reconstruction options described include cross-facial nerve grafting, nerve transfers, end-to-end nerve repair, gracilis free muscle transfer and static procedures.[1] The surgical anatomy of the face, including the superficial musculo-aponeurotic system (SMAS), has been described as relevant to corrective surgery for facial palsy.[2]
Rehabilitation techniques such as Kabat rehabilitation, photobiomodulation and electrical stimulation are the subject of registered trials in Bell's palsy.[3][4][5]

Neurectomy in this context generally refers to selectively cutting nerve branches, for example to reduce overactivity on the unaffected or synkinetic side so that the face looks more balanced. The sources reviewed do not describe neurectomy outcomes, and it is not covered further here.

A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial studied prednisolone and valaciclovir in Bell's palsy.[6] Several trials of rehabilitation and physical therapies are registered, including Kabat rehabilitation versus conventional physical therapy (n=36),[3] Kabat versus neural mobilisation (completed, n=28),[7] photobiomodulation for idiopathic facial paralysis (completed, n=96),[4] and photobiomodulation with electrical stimulation (not yet recruiting).[5] A registered trial of deep-plane facelift as a staged adjunct to facial reanimation is also listed.[8] The sources reviewed give no published outcomes for these registrations.

card.summary: Medical and surgical care for asymmetry caused by facial nerve paralysis; an established clinical field, not a cosmetic add-on for normal faces.
card.note: Evidence summarised here concerns paralysis patients; neurectomy outcomes were not covered by the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Facial nerve paralysis, most often from Bell's palsy, leaves one side of the face weak and can cause visible asymmetry. Treatment ranges from corticosteroids and rehabilitation to nerve and muscle surgery.

About 71% of Bell's palsy patients are reported to recover fully, and several rehabilitation trials are registered.
quick.mechanism: Drugs reduce nerve inflammation, rehabilitation techniques aim to improve movement, and surgery repairs, reroutes or replaces nerve or muscle function. Neurectomy means cutting selected nerve branches.
quick.risks: Surgical options carry the usual operative risks. Outcomes of neurectomy were not described in the sources reviewed.
